lines.text: A sixty-five-year-old widow entered a Puerto Rico emergency room with chills, cold sweat, dizziness, and chest pains. At the desk, she received a number.
The hospital's position was precise: it had not denied her screening or treatment and would have attended to her if she had waited.
But the jury heard evidence that she arrived in critical condition and received what the court called only a high number and a cold shoulder.
The court said a complete failure to attend someone showing symptoms widely understood as an acute threat can itself deny an appropriate screening.
That is constructive refusal: nobody says no, yet the system never reaches the person standing inside it asking for care.
This Short does not claim that the wait caused her death. The legal finding here concerns what happened while she waited.
EMTALA promises a screening procedure administered even-handedly, not perfect treatment and not a guarantee that every patient is seen simultaneously.
The case began with a number handed across a desk, and it ends with the same number still waiting to be called.
